items.title: akahoshi ramen — chicago, illinois
items.content_html:
this shop is widely known as one of the top, if not the top, ramen spots in chicago. did not realize that, tbh, until gabi and i went on a saturday afternoon. they open 5-9 everyday, and we were there by 5:15. by then, despite over half of the tables typically reserved for walk-ins, there was a large queue which took us 2 hours to overcome. i was starving, but i honestly wanted to get ramen and we were already there.

but, soon enough, we were sitting down in a long bench and quickly got our food. i ordered the standard Akahoshi Miso ramen. to be honest, im no ramen connoisseur by any means. i just really like ramen without much understanding about its complexities. i don’t know exactly what kinds of ramen i like and what kinds i don’t, but this new #category is what im here to discover for myself.

so, back to the miso ramen. honestly, it was the best ramen i’ve had in months. the noodles were bouncy and had a good, squiggly texture. the chashu was absolutely amazing: tender, balanced, charred, wonderful. definitely one of my most memorable chashu place along with Ramenwell in SF I had years ago. the other toppings were great: bean sprouts kept a nice crunch and the green onion provided the needed freshness and balance. the broth, though, was a bit light—surprising for this mixed miso broth as i thought it’d be more heavy, fermented, strong. other than that, great!

overall, would definitely revisit and try a different tare ramen. i don’t think im a huge miso ramen guy but they did it well enough that i enjoyed it without any issue. the owner/chef seems like a great, helpful, and warm part of the ramen community (esp. on reddit as u/Ramen_Lord) and knows his craft well + has a soothing humbleness from what i can read.

  • noodle: 8
  • broth: 6
  • toppings: 9
  • balance: 7.5
  • satisfaction: 7.8
  • overall: 7.7

here’s my newly-started ramen review sheet

items.title: intro to personal finance, investing
items.content_html:
hi there! :) excited? i love personal finance, but i am by no means an expert. but regardless, i shall do my best with what i know to provide an easy and warm intro to future-proofing your life financially and ensuring you don’t miss TOO much of the opportunities that only time and an early start gives.

risk and return

let’s talk investing! there’s a lot of different ways to save and invest, and they vary in two aspects: risk and return. risk can be simply defined as probability of losing on your investment, and return is typically just how much you gain or earn as a percentage of your investment. if one desires a higher investment return, they must, in 99% of cases, accept more risk. for example, if you keep your money in the bank, it’s typically the most risk-free. you don’t really gain much, especially if the money is not in a high-yield savings account (HYSA). but at the same time, you don’t stand a lose it, unless the bank goes ‘rupt’. even then, FDIC (the us government) typically steps in to protect insured deposits up to $250k, so it’s pretty risk-free. on the other hand, if you had invested it all on a stock, let’s say Enphase Energy (NASDAQ: ENPH), a booming solar energy tech company that looked unstoppable in 2022, you would be looking at almost a 90% loss at the time of writing. or if you invested in NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA), you’d be up 10x on your investments. higher risk = higher reward

investing

but investing isn’t about picking the right stocks. it doesn’t have to be all luck and hope. you don’t HAVE to invest, of course, but something i read 6 years ago still stays top of mind: “investing is no longer a path to wealth, but rather a necessity for the middle class.” money devalues over time, and one of the greatest vehicles of money-making is the stock market. you don’t have to pick the right stocks, just invest in all of them! through total market funds, essentially a basket of the hundreds and thousands of the biggest companies, you’re just betting our general economy will be healthy. for example, looking simply at VT, which is Vanguard Total World Stock ETF, it has returned almost 12% on average in the last decade. $10,000 invested in 2016 would be worth ~$30,000 today. rather than betting your hard-earned dollars on a single or a few companies, which you can totally do at your own risk, you can just bet on the US market or even just the world market at large with VT. this is called index fund investing—it’s very accessible and takes less than 15 minutes to set up. see more here (in-progress).

how/where to start?

do i go on robinhood and just buy something, like VT? well yes, that works. but there’s rungs on this investing ladder, specifically there are different accounts in which you can invest within; some provide very important benefits with taxes and returns that you must take advantage of first. here’s the order i’d suggest (but read this for a more comprehensive guide):

  1. 401(k) match
    • if your employer offers you a 401(k) match, it’s free money on the table. a 401(k), in short, is a retirement account provided by most employers. it’s a “retirement” account because it provides large tax advantages if you agree on not withdrawing money until retirement age of around 59.5. there are certain situations in which you can withdraw early, so don’t worry. see here (in-progress).
    • depending on the 401(k) plan, you’d be getting some sort of % match. for example, a 100% match up to 6% of your salary. that’s literally part of your compensation, so not taking advantage of it is letting your employer keep your hard-earned money. to enroll in it, just opt-in to your 401(k) and designate at least the match percentage of each paycheck to it. assuming the match policy above, you’d want to contribute 6% of each paycheck to your 401(k), and your employer will double that contribution each time!
    • what’s so good about a 401(k) besides the match?? read bullet #3!
  2. Roth IRA
    • so, this is still a retirement account, but it’s a personal one, rather than tied to employment/employer. anybody can open one! the only constraint is: you need to have earned income w/in IRS’s annual limit of ~$165,000 if filing single or ~$246,000 if filing jointly at the time of writing. so you need to have legal, documented, and taxed income haha.
    • once you meet that requirement, you’re good to go, and boy is this a phenomenal investment account. here’s why (inspired from Fidelity):
      1. money will grow tax-free, withdrawals are also tax-free! you use post-tax money (which is money already on hand/in your bank/etc.) to contribute to Roth IRA; that’s the only tax part of it, rest is tax-free!
      2. there are no required minimum distributions (meaning you’re not forced to withdraw a certain amount after a certain age unlike 401(k)s, etc. which is helpful to more intentionally plan your taxable income amount in later years)
      3. you can ALWAYS withdraw your contributions at any time! other retirement accounts like 401(k) may have penalties for withdrawal early outside a qualified event, like a first home purchase.
    • because it’s so tax-advantaged and flexible, the government sets a limit to how much you can contribute. for 2026, it is $7,500! that’s why you want to maximize your contribution to this every year that you can. the tax benefits are insane.
    • here’s Fidelity’s more comprehensive explanation of a Roth IRA!
  3. 401(k)
    • so, there’s two types of 401(k) usually: Roth vs Traditional. a Roth 401(k), like a Roth IRA, takes post-tax money (so money after income tax, etc.) of your paycheck and invests it so that it grows tax-free! a Traditional 401(k) uses pre-tax money (takes it out of paycheck so you don’t pay taxes on that portion of your paycheck) and invests it, but taxes you on the capital gains (not your contribution, but only the gains) when you withdraw.
    • you can decide what’s best for you! i contribute to both types because i want more tax flexibility in the future. traditional allows me to avoid some taxes today, and i plan on converting it to roth ira after leaving my employer and during low-income years (this is a bit more complex, you can read more here later (in-progress), but ignore for now)
    • to make things simple for you, just do a traditional 401(k) first and you can always change your mind later! both options gives you tax breaks, just differently.
  4. HSA
    • HSA, or a health savings account, is something i haven’t started yet. it’s another tax-advantaged account that is meant to pay for qualified medical expenses, including co-pays, dental care, contacts, and more! however, you NEED a HSA-eligible plan, aka a high-deductible health plan (HDHP) to have an HSA.
    • it’s super tax-advantages, often referred to as triple tax-advantaged:
      1. firstly, it typically uses pre-tax contributions, which gives you a tax break on that part of your paycheck, similar to a traditional 401(k) contribution. however, it’s actually better in that it not only avoids income tax, but also the FICA tax (which is payroll tax for social security and medicare)!
      2. secondly, growth within the account is tax-free (except for a few states like new jersey and cali)!
      3. lastly, withdrawals for qualified medical expenses (which are pretty flexible and includes things like massage guns, wearable health devices, skincare, and much more) are tax-free! sephora even has a whole section for HSA-eligible products (over 170 products at time of writing)
  5. taxable brokerage
    • then, the last place to park your investing money (of these options of course and to the best of my knowledge) would be a taxable brokerage. that just means no particular special investment account like a 401(k) or IRA, but rather your good old-fashioned brokerage account like on Robinhood, Charles Schwab, and also Fidelity/Vanguard, which typically houses a lot of retirement accounts too!
    • the cons of a regular, taxable brokerage is just that there’s no tax advantages. no pre-tax contributions. no tax-free growth. no tax-free withdrawals. but hey! you’re only getting taxed on money earned anyways, not on contributions and not on losses (T.T), so tax isn’t necessarily a bad thing; it means you’re at least making some money haha.

okay, all that being said, one important note: just putting money into these accounts doesn’t mean you’re necessarily investing! you have to actually choose funds or stocks to invest in, and that goes back to the idea of index fund investing. a very common and easy index fund investing setup would be the Bogleheads' Three-Fund Portfolio, which uses three funds (hence the name): 1) a domestic total market fund, 2) an international total market fund, and 3) a bond total market fund. assuming you’re under 40, i’d skip the bond fund and just do a two-fund portfolio. as for the two funds, i would suggest 70% VTI (Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF) and 30% VXUS (Vanguard Total International Stock ETF). the former is a fund comprises of ~3,500+ U.S. companies with a low expense ratio of 0.03% and the latter comprises of over 8000+ companies with an expense ratio of 0.05%. of course, there are many other portfolios you can go with, but this is just a typical one with a balanced risk-return profile. you can definitely go safer by adding a bond fund or cash position, and you can go riskier by buying more concentrated funds like QQQ (tracks the NASDAQ 100, aka the 100 largest companies on the NASDAQ exchange) or even individual stocks!

that’s all for today! more to be written

items.title: galbitang 갈비탕 (beef short rib soup) [instant pot]
items.content_html:
source/inspo: Korean Bapsang

yap over the holidays, gabi and i decided to buy a multicooker (an Instant Pot, colloquially) for funsies, mostly because i thought it’d make meals and prepping easier! in particular, we wanted to make broths and soups; thus, this became the first recipe we followed, and it was great!

ingredients (4 servings) we halved it for ourselves!

  • 3 to 4 pounds beef short ribs
  • 1 medium onion cut into halves
  • 2 large scallions white parts
  • 8 plump garlic cloves (or 1 whole bulb) If using bulb, cut into halves crosswise
  • 3 thin ginger slices 1-inch rounds
  • 2 tablespoons soup soy sauce
  • salt and pepper
  • 1 pound Korean radish cut into bite size pieces (about 1.5-inch square, ⅓ - inch thick)
  • 3 ounces starch noodles dangmyeon, soaked in warm water for 30 minutes - optional
  • 2 scallions, finely chopped garnish

steps

  1. first trim off any thick layer of surface fat on the ribs
  2. then, in a pot, rinse them in cold water a few times to remove surface blood + bone dust
  3. drain then fill the pot w/ enough water to cover the ribs, about 4 cups
  4. close the lid tightly, turn on manual + high pressure for 2 minutes, ensure pressure switch turned to “sealing/sealed”
  5. once done, discard the liquid (or save to use in the soup or future meals). strain to remove brown bits if you’re using it though! then, thoroughly rinse ribs and the pot clean.
  6. return ribs to pot, add the onion, garlic, ginger, and soup soy sauce. add about 10 cups of water (ensure it’s below max fill line). then close lid tightly and pressure cook ribs for 35-40 minutes depending on thickness. NPR 10 minutes.
  7. once done, remove ribs, remove aromatic veggies w/ strainer, skim off fat
  8. then, put ribs back in along w/ cut radishes. change instant pot setting to “saute” and boil until radish turns translucent (about 10 min after boiling)
  9. add optional noodles a couple minutes before turning instant pot off. we cooked the noodles separately
  10. salt and pepper to taste! skim off or use fat separator to remove remaining fat if served hot. or just chill soup and discard the solidified fat. garnish w/ chopped scallions to serve!

tips

  • the strained cooking liquid in step 5 can make the soup taste more “beefy” if added back in!
  • removing scum and fat early on helps keep the broth clear and clean
  • a good soup soy sauce makes a big difference in the taste. you can also use light fish sauce or regular soy sauce, but the latter can make the soup very dark, so use small amount and season w/ salt
  • gabi recommends to still soak the short ribs beforehand to reduce the fat/scum in the initial cooking, making it easier to clean and continue onwards!

items.title: LOT Polish 787-8 Business Class Review
items.content_html:
This past Sunday, Gabi and I had the opportunity to ride business class on LOT Polish from Chicago to Krakow. They fly this route once weekly with the rest of the week to Warsaw.

I don’t believe there’s any other airline that flies direct from Chicago to Poland just yet, and I think the reason why LOT flies it is because Chicago boasts an impressive Polish and people with Polish ancestry population. It’s to the point where a 2023 study by the city found Polish to be the 4th most widely spoken language in Chicago behind English, Spanish, and Mandarin. What’s interesting is that the 1972 musical Grease had the majority of characters with Polish surnames based on real-life experiences in a Chicago high school, but subsequent productions and films have toned down the Chicago Polish influences.

Anyways, back to the flight, we’re flying non-revenue standby, so we didn’t have confirmed tickets yet. We needed to clear with the ticketing counter for standby boarding passes, then we’d have to go to the gate to clear for actual seats. The loads had looked good, and we had little issue with it all. Security check at ORD Terminal 5 was awful as it was around 9pm and the PreCheck/Clear lines were all closed. It went from 4 security lines to 1 combined one, and it took us 45 minutes to get through. Our standby passes had “Fast Track” but it was just for show haha. Good thing we had enough time. Once boarding almost finished, the gate agent issued us our confirmed boarding passes: 1A and 1B! Not only business class, but also sitting next to each other without having to explicitly ask! To be fair, the cabin was only 2/3rds full.

So, LOT Polish still has the common but outdated 2-2-2 business class layout. That means 33% of business class passengers do not have direct access to the aisle and would likely need to climb over or wake up a sleeping passenger to use the restroom or exit their seats. However, what’s nice about it is that it felt a lot more open and spacious. The seats seemed noticeable wider with more legroom, which Gabi enjoyed a lot. The lack of wifi was honestly a fresh change of pace; I’ve missed the forced disengagement from the digital world air travel used to have. However, this layout and older product definitely can invite more awkwardness if sitting with strangers due to the limited divider and shared middle tray. Some other cons was that the seats lacked accessible storage space with only the foot cabinet space (unreachable if secured with a seatbelt) and overhead bins as storage. The entertainment devices were also quite outdated, and we ended up not using them at all. There was also this annoying, bright green light that I could not understand having.

The food was pretty solid, though! That was a relief as we didn’t have dinner. For the appetizer, I chose the green asparagus cream soup, and I really enjoyed it! Baked rib eye with mashed potatoes and veggies was my main of choice. The meat was on the drier end, but only slightly, and it was overall well-seasoned and tasty. The drinks kept flowing non-stop—great Polish hospitality. Had mostly blackcurrant and orange juice haha, but I’m sure their wine selection was great. Tons of dessert options. Breakfast was also good. The cafe latte, though, tasted evidently like powdered espresso. I’m not sure how Turkish Airlines had such good espresso for their catering.

After dinner, we set the beds ourselves. I’m sure they would’ve helped if requested, but it honestly was pretty simple. The mattress cover was more for cleanliness than comfort—quite thin. Blanket—also quite thin—was enough comfort, although on the shorter side (not for me given average height). Pillow was solid. Gabi slept really well. I woke up a few times, mostly due to light coming from the gallery. I really should’ve used the nice eye mask I keep with me 24/7 or not have dropped the one they gave me. My fault. Overall, solid and roomy sleep experience.

At the end of the day, it was a relaxing and pleasant time. We had a great flight attendant taking care of us. She definitely helped elevate the experience, especially by stating that she was really happy to have had us as passengers (made my day). We all bonded over the cute Kodak Charmera we were taking photos with. Everyone was nice and helpful overall, too! It’s no Turkish Airlines in terms of hard and soft business class product, but it definitely was a memorable experience all the same.

items.title: Cities and Ambition — Paul Graham (2008)
items.content_html:
Cities and Ambition ~3,600 words ~12 min read

alice sent me this, and it was an interesting read despite almost a decade passing since it was authored. i do see new york, sf, and berkeley reflect what he considered the messages of his time: focus on wealth, focus on power/prestige, and focus on living well. i would say that boston perhaps has not lived up to his expectations, but i also know nothing of boston really. what i suspect, though, is that intellectual production has shifted globally as the world adapted to a more digitally-connected world. many with ideas, creativity, and hunger for knowledge have been seemingly bypassing academia altogether and going straight into industry. chicago, where i am currently based, is interesting. it seems a bit more balanced and friendly. less comparison with one another and more focused on simply enjoying life? the conversations i’ve had here are much less clustered around wealth, prestige, and ambition, which has been a calm change of pace.

however, i’ve definitely not settled into the city yet to be comfortable saying too much about it. it’s been a bit hard to, especially as i knew very little people coming in. i also haven’t been intentional at all with it—mores o escaping abroad or spending time with my girlfriend in lieu of building a strong foundation in chicago. part of me also feels like my stay here is temporary, which makes me hesitant of planting and nurturing seeds in the city. but, i understand it is still all worth doing as relationships are the crux of life’s enjoyment. i just gotta set my mind to it and execute haha.

items.title: CUBIC3 Coffee 三立方咖啡 — Shanghai, China
items.content_html:
there’s so many coffee chains in shanghai! most notably, i see Manner Coffee and Luckin Coffee literally everywhere, but i honestly haven’t tried them yet. coffee hasn’t been my drink of choice lately, which sucks because i created this coffee category for it. i’ve come to realize that i should still take pictures of cute cafes, but not necessarily review the food/drink if unneeded. it’s likely that these cafes won’t be here in a few years anyways or that the quality of beans and whatnot change quickly.

all that being said, i found a spot in shanghai i couldn’t resist trying out: CUBIC3 Coffee (三立方咖啡 locally)! this particular shop was the 兆丰广场店 location.

how’s the coffee you might ask? well, no oat milk, so cannot compare to my usual. it was honestly fine, nothing to write home about; just a solid iced latte. the architecture, though, was really pretty. i enjoyed the minimalist x brutalist design with the spaciousness within. it’s also super cool that you can roast your own mix of coffee beans from all around the world! overall, would come back to it! esp. to just relax. it’s right next to a park!!!!

items.title: KIELO COFFEE Asakusa — Tokyo, Japan
items.content_html:
this is one of three stores that kielo coffee has! the main store has over 1,000 reviews and still sits at 4.7 stars! was a cute little space, not too much seating, had a bit of a wait (likely because where the asakusa store was situated is high traffic, low specialty coffee presence). a strong amount of tourists as well.

i thought the presentation was very cute, and there were a lot of interesting beans to choose from + some pastries! some of the beans can be sold out just fyi, and they have a little setup where you can smell each bean before choosing. the price was a bit shocking for japan imo, ranging from $5 to $12 for a cup of coffee. i liked that they had a little bean profile card that accompanied your drink. i definitely will say that i could taste unique notes in my coffee, although they weren’t to my preference. but overall, good experience! the staff were outgoing and sweet. the presentation, esp. outside of my simple order, was pleasant. i think my order simply didn’t allow for the full experience of the specialty beans as it is an iced latte at the end of the day :)

items.title: 20% to FIRE!
items.content_html:
I did have to force myself to look under all the cushions to get there. It definitely sounds nicer than it is, especially with the heck of a bull market in the past 6 months. I know the market is very regularly near all-time highs, and it’s hard to understand what the new normal really is. Is it normal to experience hyperinflation? Is it normal to have your government shut down for weeks? Is it normal to look at the news and just see only hate, violence, pedophilia, drama, death, and prejudice? Is it normal that many of my friends who just graduated college struggle so hard to find even one job in their field of interest? Is it normal that AI dependence, both administratively and emotionally, is seeming to grow at an exponential rate? Is it normal that I feel disappointed in our world? I guess it’s better than being in a global war? At least we’re decaying internally.

It just feels like this FIRE journey is one of pure optimism. Such is the need for the dollar to stop devaluing. Such is the need for everything to stop becoming so abhorrently more expensive everyday. Such is the need for companies to prioritize social benefits over shareholder value and profit. Such is the need for politicians care about their constituents.

Every single day. Goodbye Social Security. Goodbye SNAP disbursements. Goodbye Medicaid. Goodbye political cooperation. Goodbye social unity.

What kind of safety net is needed to feel safe?

Probably the kind that you don’t need to work for? The kind you already have? Sighs, the envy for the more privileged is up-surfacing again. I should probably go figure out what that means. Security as a birthright versus security as a lifelong project are two different lives completely I feel. And that feeling scares me as I question whether this pursuit of security has instead left something in the wayside. Something that only at the point of a self-decided point of security I then realize I had lost in the process. The pursuit of happiness? The pursuit of personal interest? The pursuit of the arts? I have no clue. I try to balance it all. I try to be intentional about being intentional, so that these regrets don’t happen.

But, to be free already at birth. Isn’t that a beauty?

items.title: on writing
items.content_html: how does one write in this day and age? what is the value of knowing how to thoughtfully construct words and phrases? is there value to be had in training this skillset? will the future of technology render those countless hours useless? because in this world of ever-decreasing attention span focused on visually-engaging short-form video content, it feels like writing gets left in the dust. i’m wrong though. writing is part of this new generation of content. in fact, writing i’d say is instrumental in it all. i want to be a good writer. i want to be proud of how i encapsulate and express my thoughts into written form. but writing is hard. writing, for me, requires intention, patience, and a certain type of peace. i can’t fully put my finger on what kind of peace i mean. but the type that temporarily blocks all my worries, insecurities, stress, anxieties, fears, and restlessness for just a moment. many are artificial, borne by the environment and society that surrounds me. worries about money. insecurities about self-worth. stress about time and experiences slipping away. anxieties about my relationships or lack there of. fears about my well-being and productivity at work. restlessness about the state of the world, the state of our society, and the state of our future. when we look at humanity from above, what do we see? why don’t we seem to have a shared purpose that unites us all? what are we doing with our lives? the little blips of time and space that we occupy. one blip we’re here. one blip we’re gone. one more blip we’re forgotten. into dust and the vacuum of space. what do we anchor ourselves to then? it seems so easy to get lost in it all. i get lost often. writing, i’m hoping, will be one of my small anchors. but, how does one write? how do we return the favor to those who choose to spend their own time, and thus lifespan, in reading one’s writing? it can’t just be rambling, can it? luckily, i’m just writing to myself. i hope future me won’t be too harsh of a critic. i’m young and a bit adrift. and most importantly, i think i miss my friends. also, working sucks. i really like my team. my manager is super nice and knowledgeable. the other analysts are very cool and smart. the projects are quite interesting. the office is quite neat and modern. the culture is great, warm, and supportive. but working… argh.

items.title: re: Mega Backdoor Roth
items.content_html:
Let’s talk about the Mega Backdoor Roth! Note that only some employers allow for this as it’s 1) more expensive 2) more complex 3) more overhead in general 4) targeted towards higher earners only

Pleasantly surprising, United Airlines has this baked into our Fidelity 401(k) plan, which I, despite being a bit too low-earning to fully take advantage of it, will try it out.

What is a Mega Backdoor Roth? So, this is a retirement strategy that comprises of two features inside a 401(k) plan to get tens of thousands more dollars into Roth status (meaning it can grow tax-free FOREVER!), far beyond the traditional ~$7k Roth IRA limit.

Those two features, which again may not be available for all 401(k) plans, are after-tax 401(k) contributions and Roth in-plan conversion. The former is a third contribution type after traditional pre-tax and Roth. The latter is the ability to roll this after-tax money out to a Roth IRA while still employed. With both, one can execute the Mega Backdoor Roth.

A 2022 report by Plan Sponsor Council of America found that only 21% of 401(k) plans allow after-tax contributions, and that’s only one of two mechanisms needed for this to work. I’d guess only 10-15% of 401(k) plans fully enable this strategy.

IRS Limits So, let’s talk about limits. 401(k) contributions are known to have a ~$23,500 cap. However, that only applies to pre-tax and Roth 401(k) contributions only. There’s actually a further limit of ~$69,000 which includes pre-tax and Roth, as well as employer match and after-tax! This means you can contribute after-tax contributions to your 401(k) even after meeting the $23,500 pre-tax and Roth cap. You don’t necessarily have to wait until you reach that $23,500 cap to start doing after-tax contribution. It’s just that it’s best to fully take advantage of the $23,500 pre-tax/Roth contributions first as it is the most tax-efficient and allows for essentially free money w/ employer match. I personally plan to do a percentage for pre-tax and after-tax on each paycheck for now as to not need a mid-year manual adjustment. Fidelity also helps cut the contributions off if they are set to go over the limits, which further reduces needed headspace.

Flow Paycheck → After-tax 401(k) → Roth in-plan conversion (inside 401(k) plan) → Grows tax-free as Roth 401(k) → Leave employer → Rollover Roth 401(k) to personal Roth IRA (no deadline, but never hurts to do it sooner than later) → No RMDs, Lifetime Tax-Free Growth

Summary Even among the financially-literate, many think the annual Roth contribution limit is strictly capped at ~$7,000. But inside certain 401(k) plans, this Mega Backdoor Roth strategy allows the conversion of up to $40,000+ per year into Roth status… tax-free forever. It’s lowkey ridiculous, but hey, enjoy it while it lasts. As for me, I do not get paid enough yet to fully partake in it, but that’s a me problem, not a you problem :D

items.title: niku udon (beef udon)
items.content_html:
source/inspo: Just One Cookbook

another comfort food!

ingredients (4 servings)

  • 1 tokyo negi? aka long green onion or 4 reg green onions(white part only)
  • 2 green onion / scallion (for topping)
  • 16 oz thinly sliced beef (like ribeye)
  • 2 tbsp neutral oil
  • 4 tsp sugar
  • 2 tbsp soy sauce
  • 4 servings udon! (1000g frozen udon or 360g dry udon)

broth

  • 5 cups dashi (2.5 tsp hondashi then? usually i do 1 tsp to 1 cup for full base stuff like miso, but here we alr have lots of other salt/umami already)
  • 3 tbsp soy sauce
  • 2 tbsp mirin
  • 2 tsp sugar
  • 0.25 tsp diamond crystal kosher salt (j for consistency apparently, if morton salt, use like 1/8 tsp instead)

broth steps

  1. 5 cups dashi broth to a low boil for 1-2 min -> then season w/ the soy sauce, mirin, sugar, and fancy salt (cover w/ lid to keep hot & prevent evaporation) & turn off heat after 1-2 min

meat steps

  1. cut white part of negi into 1/2 inch diagonal slices
  2. cut 2 green onion into thin slices for garnish
  3. heat frying pan and when hot, add 2 tbsp oil + negi and saute until golden brown n tender
  4. then add the beef, cook until not pink, and now add the 4 tsp sugar and 2 tbsp soy sauce
  5. stir-fry until well coated and then remove from heat

final steps

  1. make and drain udon (typically like 1 min to reheat w/ boil for frozen udon)
  2. portion udon in bowls + pour hot broth into them
  3. place stir-fried beef into bowls + season them w/ green onions

tips

  • for broth, can add 1/2 tsp white soy (shiro shoyu) at end for cleaner, more delicate finish perhaps? never tried
  • can marinate beef beforehand by tossing it w/ 1 tsp soy + 1 tsp mirin + pinch sugar for 10 min before cooking
  • can deglaze pan w/ 1-2 tbsp of hot broth after cooking + pour back into broth
  • for more veggies, add bokchoy & napa (add after broth seasoning + simmer for ~5 min before turning off fire) or spinach (at end, blanch w/ hot broth for 15s until bright green/wilted then immediately portion)
  • also at end for serving, can drizzle w/ sesame oil or add poached egg or maybe like crispy shallots/onions

items.title: how early should we arrive to the airport?
items.content_html:
currently reading gad allon’s post about when to arrive at airports (typing as i go, so it’s not going to be the most organized/concise/well-written). he introduces this idea of the newsvendor problem where a newsvendor has to decide how many newspaper to stock each day w/o knowing exact demand. hitting average means high stockouts or excess inventory, and the proposed solution is choosing a quantile of the demand distribution determined by relative cost of each outcome.

so for this airport arrival, studies have found that security wait times are let’s say 20 minutes. to calculate the cumulative distribution of waiting time b/w arrival to gate (F_s), we do C_o / (C_o + C_u) with Co being cost of overage or cost per minute of waiting too long and with Cu being one-time penealty of being late. we then input into F_s L*, which is the optimal arrival buffer or the quantile of the distribution that balances those costs.

thus, averages are misleading as you’d likely be in the 90th-99th percentile where the lower range would be for leisure and higher range would be time-sensitive, high-premium travel. you, as a passenger, would likely not be in 50th percentile as underage cost can be ridiculously expensive as we see with my dear friend Hope who had to pay an exorbitant fare to take the next international flight out to make it back home in time for work a month or so ago. as for the overage cost, even if we assume $100,000 average annual income at ~$48/hr, the additional hour, let’s say, is marginal, especially considering time spent in lounges or browsing shops, which may reduce the perceived cost of overage.

rational travelers optimize to higher quantiles, not the mean, as cost of missing a flight would likely easily dwarf the cost of waiting, especially for international flights.

so, yes, on average, you don’t have to be 2 hours early. but the variance remains too high and the underage cost too daunting that the safest strategy is as the century-old newsvendor says: overstock. whether it be time or newspaper, you’d rather have extra on hand than none at a time of desperation.

for myself, i almost always arrive quite early at international airports abroad. i try to aim for at least an hour between post-security/immigration and boarding, allowing me some time to explore the airport, grab some drinks and maybe food at lounges (w/ priority pass [essentially only valuable abroad]), and prepare all my offline entertainment. for domestic flights, i try to aim to be past security right as we start boarding. there’s no valuable lounge access that i have, and i’m less intrigued by domestic airports. however, aiming for that has led me to arrive at airports like SFO in the middle of boarding, yet I still somehow made it through security & onto my international flights ontime. tbf, they were all cases of poor route time estimation by uber + unplanned traffic incidents + optimistic time buffers; thus, that’s why you aim for the 90th+ percentile, not 50th. anyways, as for airport dad, i’m more convinced he doesn’t want to suffer emotional and mental exhaustion of post-missed-flight drama and chaos rather than the financial damage.

source: gad allon’s article

first time typing on the morning bus to work. it’s really not the most conducive experience, but it works! today seems to be the last warm day for a small stretch of time. it’s a high of 85 degrees today, and the rest of the week I think should be around a high of low 70s.

thinking of what i want to type in my morning bus rides. what kinds of mentions, descriptions, or thoughts would i appreciate reading back on in a few years?

i guess that would be my current dilemmas of life. i’m going to work in an industry i never expected to join in the first place. i lack the pre-requisite knowledge that many of my peers here have gained as a byproduct of their hobbies and interests. i’m put into a role that necessitates large contextual understanding of not just the company but the industry as a whole. i really appreciate my team, but i fear that i’m honestly not much of a value-add. i have a large project that honestly is so simple yet so complex; it’s a struggle to get through. i feel again a bit disjointed about work. not sure if that’s even an accurate way to describe my feeling. may dictionary it later.

the perks are great. just came back from istanbul with gabi. got to sit business class in a foreign carrier, and, my goodness, was it amazing for <$400 a person.

i’m not quite sure what’s the next step for me. it feels like i just started, yet it also feels like i need to think a bit ahead regardless.

part of me is missing school. the ease of friends. the ease of new friends. the prioritization of education. the constant chaos + flurry of activity. perhaps a masters would be a fun next step if i choose to pivot into another industry that necessitates that step.

items.title: gyudon (japanese beef rice bowl)
items.content_html:
source/inspo: Just One Cookbook

gyudon is one of my favorite japanese comfort foods: thinly sliced beef and onions simmered in a sweet-savory sauce, served over hot rice. it’s quick, easy to make, and just so tasty.

ingredients (4 servings)

  • 1 onion (about 8 oz)
  • 2 green onions
  • 1 lb thinly sliced beef (ribeye / short plate is my go-to)
  • cooked rice
  • optional: pickled red ginger for topping

sauce

  • 1 cup dashi (~0.53 tsp hondashi)
  • 4 tbsp sake (or chinese rice wine / water)
  • 4 tbsp mirin (or 4 tbsp water + 4 tsp sugar)
  • 6 tbsp soy sauce
  • 2 tbsp sugar (to taste)

steps

  1. thinly slice onion + green onion (diagonally)
  2. in a pan (off heat), mix dashi, sake, mirin, soy sauce, sugar (ensure sugar & hondashi is mostly dissolved)
  3. add onions into the broth & spread evenly. then, place beef slices on top.
  4. cover, turn on fire and bring to a simmer on medium, then lower heat and cook 3–4 minutes. skim off foam/scum as needed/wanted!
  5. sprinkle green onion, cook 1 more minute. also, good time to add beaten eggs if that’s something you’d like. i’ve never tried tbh.
  6. serve over hot rice with sauce, garnish with pickled ginger if desired (me personally, not a fan).

tips

  • great w/ sides like miso soup or a small salad
  • add toppings at the end like toasted sesame seeds or seaweed?
  • if u want more veggies/greens, you can add bokchoy or napa cabbage w/ onions or spinach at the end and stir for 30-60 secs.

items.title: Turkish Airlines 787-9 Business Class Review
items.content_html:
Beyond all odds, we made it to the business cabin on Turkish. We weren’t supposed to, but a stroke of luck made it fruition. Originally, they were out of business class seats. There were technically 2 seats unbooked, but that’s because they were inoperable, thus unfit and unavailable for passenger use. Somehow, the gate agents didn’t see those indicators and gave us boarding passes for them without letting us know about those issues.

When we got onboard, the in-flight crew was confused regarding the gate agents hadn’t let us know about the issues when issuing the tickets. I mentioned perhaps it’s because we’re non-revenue standby (thus second-class citizens haha), but they said it doesn’t matter and that we had the right to know. At this point, I was worried we were out of these seats, but they somehow made it work. I sat in 8A with an inoperable storage nook, which was a very minor issue for me. I get why they wouldn’t want a revenue customer experiencing that though. Gabi, originally in a seat with a broken table, ended up moving to a fully-functional seat in 1A that someone ended up not making. How fortunate for us, and I do hope the missing passenger ended up making his way to where he needed.

But, every non-revenue passenger knows (or will come to know) one vital rule: the job ain’t done until you’re in the air. You can definitely get pulled off the plane for any reason: load and balance issues, overbooking issues and last-minute revenue passengers, recently-discovered inoperable seats, and many more. So, it’s always wise to not celebrate too early. However, once we pushed back, I sighed with relief and satisfaction. We took off soundly and started making our way back to Chicago.

Now, let’s dive to the review:

cabin & seat

this felt like your typical modern business cabin—a 1-2-1 layout with individual, privatized seats. comparable to United Polaris I’d say, although I think Turkish does it just slightly better with their materials. They used Alcantara padding in the interior trimming of the seats, which is suede-like material typically used in fancy schmancy cars. overall, a great and solid hard product.

service & crew

this was my first time flying non-rev business on a different airline, so i felt a bit out of place and anxious. however, the crew were very professional and well-spoken, whereas LOT Polish’s (in a future review) were very warm. both styles are great in their own ways.

food & beverage

oh my goodness. gabi and i have never been so enthralled and over the moon with our flying experience until this one. the menu was so frickin' long and had so much variety.

drinks: the juices, oh, were so delicious. they tasted like they squeezed it straight in the galley, which i really doubt, but the taste had me super super second-guessing. gabi had a smoothie, and she said it was “so delicious, tasted like blended fresh, still had the pulpiness of my fruits in it, super fresh and sweet but not in a sugary way.” i also had an iced latte with oat milk, and it was SUCH a solid iced latte (like 6/10) ON A PLANE! CRAZY! gabi downed gallons of turkish tea she said, and they were great as they usually are. other options on the table were mocktails, detox drinks, 5 different wellness tea, homemade lemonade, and more! bunch of wine options, but i haven’t acquired that taste just yet.

food: the food, though, was also top-tier. a literal CHEF with a chef hat and robes pushed a silver cart down the aisle and served me SEATSIDE. SO COOL. i loved the “creamy turmeric cauliflower soup” that was ladled to me right then and there, and there were such an assortment of other appetizers like roast beef roll, salmon gravlax, traditional Turkish cheese “börek”, and more. but what broke me was the “Braised lamb shank with Mediterranean vegtables, celeriac mousseline, thyme jus, Chimichurri sauce” because i’m not much a lamb guy, but that was easily top 3, if not 1, lamb dishes i’ve ever had. it was fall-apart tender (my bone literally fell apart from the meat, it was shocking) and so delicious. the sauces accentuated the lamb so much too!!! so well-plated as well. goodness, i was in such disbelief. for dessert, i had some lovely Turkish ice cream and fresh fruit. the fresh fruit, again, was SO FRESH and SO GOOD. i had like 4 or 5 cups of fresh fruit. it was too too good. how do i say this? SO SO SO GOOD. for breakfast, i also had yogurt with fresh fruits and homemade granola as well as pancakes with caramelized apples. also absolutely delicious i tell you. i initially slept past breakfast, but they offered it to me when i woke up bless up thank you Turkish.

oh also, Turkish Airlines has been bragging about having the oldest bread onboard from 12,000 years ago. i was hyped for it as i love bread. ngl, it was solid bread but quite grainy (i liked it just fine, but gabi was underwhelmed LOL)

ife, amenities, and others

ife was great and modern. large screen and great interface. lots of movies/shows to watch, and i especially loved the access to various cameras on the exterior of the aircraft. that was a super cool feature. amenities—nothing special. 1GB of data was provided as business-class passengers. it was slow and emptied quickly, which i expected as much haha. we are, after all, flying around the globe.

sleep & in-flight experience

after dining, the crew offered to make our beds while we changed into the provided pjs in the bathroom. came back to a thin mattress pad, nice lil pillow, and a plush blanket. slept very well :)

overall

9.5/10. the dining, as others have said, was a production. it was amazing. i don’t even know where the 0.5 deduction is going towards LOL especially since im a non-rev. i didnt mind the inoperable storage cubby at all. everything else blew my mind away.

ps: i wrote this in parts, hence the different capitalization style LOL

items.title: Symphony Coffee & Food & Bar — Brussels, Belgium
items.content_html:
Symphony Coffee & Food & Bar Zwijnaardsesteenweg 2, 9000 Gent, Belgium

good, spacious cafe right near to the Citadelpark and STAM museum! seems like a nice place to sit down and work. lots of sitting area, and the ambience felt good. when we went, there was only a few other people. we were hungry, so we just got some sandwiches.

sandwiches were really good, but also very expensive for what they were. but europe, this being my first time in northern europe, has been quite expensive throughout. oh well.

the BEST part was the cashier/server. he was such a chiller. he chatted with us and about our trip thus far! very nice guy. he also came by after we finished eating to show us a magic trick! i was like, ofc, but i made sure to try to keep an eye out for any sleight of hand tricks and whatnot. gabi and i both got a card from his deck. he shuffled it a bunch, many different ways. i couldn’t see any sleight of hand T.T i checked that he cut properly too. he found gabis card first, and we tracked it as he put it aside pretty reasonably far. then he did a fun little between the hands through the air shuffle before shuffling more and pulling out a card. i was fully expecting it to be my card, king of diamonds. turns out it was gabi’s card again!! four of clovers. then he went back to the card that was put aside, flipped it over, and it was my card??? absolute cinema.

anyways, experience and food was unforgettable. thank you strange Ghentian magician.

items.title: my overnight FlixBus experience
items.content_html:
so I saw that FlixBus had an overnight trip to Ghent which was notably cheaper than flights or train, especially since it basically cuts out one night of hotels, but oh was that the apparently common first-timer disillusion. right when I got onto the FlixBus, I googled whether they wake you up for your stop on an overnight, and an article about hey DONT DO OVERNIGHT FLIXBUSES popped up 😭 apparently, my expectation of sleeping soundly for 7 hours was false and again a beginners’ mistake, esp for young travelers. however, the article only said the chairs were not meant for sleeping, but I thought it was totally fine. if I could sleep in economy in an airline, I can sleep in these coach buses that recline 5x as much.

BUT, TURNS OUT THAT WASNT THE ISSUE. first, the bus was quite warm at 10 in the evening, but it cooled once we took off. then, people behind us just kept yapping nonstop, like it’s 10pm guys 😭. next, it was just so awkward to find a good position to sleep but that’s normal. the real next issue was finally getting some sleep, only to be woken up 40 minutes later by someone because we were deboarding to get security checked at Dover (southeastern port of 🇬🇧). got a nice passport stamp though! THEN, i found out we were going on a ferry (as you can tell, little research was put into what this bus ride entailed) on which we had to deboard and go on the passenger decks!! honestly the ferry was rly nice, got free hot food, duty-free shops, and some time to wash up in someplace other than a coach bathroom that didn’t even have running water. we had about 2 and a half hours on the ferry, so we ate a bit, shopped a bit, slept for a bit, and back on the bus we went shortly. afterwards, we nodded off and made it to Ghent too quick for comfort. but overall, that was pretty little sleep versus expectations. interesting for sure, but would i do it again? probably, im young and broke for now still. however, im truly tired and i have a whole day and work day ahead of me.

oh!! and we bought an adorable beefeater bear!

Kaffee Allez Sint-Joriskaai 6a, 9000 Gent, Belgium

first cafe post i believe despite it being at least 15 cafes since i created this category. but better late than never.

very cute cafe. right out front of a river and bridge. group of bikers gathered already at 8 in the morning out front. seems like a very cycling x coffee spot with bunch of social rides and cycling workshops being organized here! lots of indoor bike parking against the walls, too! as for coffee and pastries, pretty yums. i like how the drinks come with a little biscuit each!! the drinks across all three were quite light on the espresso though, making my iced latte quite milky—5/10. perhaps athletes and bikers that frequent prefer the lesser espresso amount. after all, too much coffee can have unappreciated aftereffects on the stomach. the croissants I quite liked, although gabi gave it 6/10 bc too doughy and structureless, id say 7.5/10. the housemade biscuit dipped into a hot drink was 10/10!

just parted ways with mimi, and it honestly feels quite devastating

a few happy points:

  • I sold it to danh, a berkeley student that I met and chatted with before who was in the same club as gabi
  • he’s an avid miata fan, and he drove mimi without hesitation and with a lot of enjoyment, consideration, and appreciation
  • he’s converting her into a manual with a mechanic friend, which honestly is a good thing; miatas are meant to be driven manual (I’ve never driven manuals, so I can’t FULLY back that up haha), and it means a lot of genuine time, effort, and care for mimi
  • he drove it down to los angeles (where his mechanic friend is) midnight the same day I handed the keys off to him + took mimi to the clouds to see the world a bit more and said that mimi was simply amazing

i honestly feel like I shouldn’t be sad. i was able to give mimi a new partner who seems to appreciate her already as much as i do. but it’s an end of an era. she was a key cornerstone to my college life and my experience in Berkeley. i drove her to visit friends, to go on dates, to see the bay from the hills, to go escape the college town and visit new spots in norcal, to play music, to talk about life, to relax, to grab groceries… to just make college life just click into place. as much as i’m sentimental, i really thought i was more prepared for this.

at first, everyone told me that it wasn’t a smart choice to get her. she had high mileage; she was older than me even; she was a small, low car, easily overlooked and hidden in blind spots; and she wasn’t practical. of course, i listened to all their inputs with consideration, but at the end, i make my own decisions, and i thought she was the one. my parents was insisting that i get the newest model if anything; i said it’s honestly her or nothing. i really didn’t care to have the means to drive. after all, i had an electric bike, electric longboard, access to a daily, free ebike-sharing program (Veo), good and discounted public transit, and two healthy legs—all in a relatively small and accessible town. my mom at the end gave in and gave me her green light. did i really need it? no, but there’s some things that as a child, you should respect. one of which is your parents' somewhat reasonable concerns about your safety. not long after Mimi became under my care, everyone started appreciating and loving her. i mean, honestly, i didn’t know what the fuss was all about in the first place. just look at her!

she showed me the joy of driving—not as a means to other enjoyment, but rather the enjoyment itself. she taught me preparedness, keeping me stocked with a portable jumper and tire inflator haha. she helped me enjoy the outdoors more, taking me to hills afar, hikes over yonder, and the stars above. she also mentored gabi how to drive, was there for her to help her pass her DMV licensure, enabled her to have a hot girl summer (whatever that means), and was always in gabi’s corner without hesitation through the ups and downs.

i’m thankful, so thankful, that i was fiscally able to take care of mimi as well. maintenance is important, yet a pretty penny at times. i do wish i learned how to take care of it all myself, but i fear i lacked the time, tools, and mental headspace during school. however, i fortunately did not lack the understanding that if i did not have the time and ability, i needed to find someone who did and compensate them for mimi’s health. i didn’t need to junk her. i didn’t need to resort to some random, potentially careless, person to take care of her next. i didn’t let her become someone’s track car throwaway.

instead, i hope, and i believe, that she will be well taken care of. she was, and still is, truly loved, and she will, to the best of my ability and hopes, continue to be loved and appreciated.

thank you mimi. for every moment. i hope you get to continue seeing the world and travel freely and fully. i shall miss you dearly, and i hope to see you again soon. i’ll learn to drive stick just for you :D

as a bit of context for the texts below, danh says Mimi, gabi and i say mimi

crazy how the real world post-education is seemingly built to overwhelm you with problems, burdens, and exhaustion that we can’t properly fight for the things we believe in and care about

i was reading Your Money or Your Life, and it mentioned about the ecological footprint. it’s been so many years since i’ve thought about it, and i did used to care and campaign for environmental change so so much more, whether it be lobbying with my fellow classmates, enacting green programs like composting on-campus, or just educating our peers what proper recycling and potential contamination was. anyways, a bit of a throwback, and i feel like it’s not an isolated problem.

i get that im more overwhelmed with worries about money and the lack of retirement options for my parents, but even my peers endowed with tens of millions or more in inheritance seem to pursue only materialism, whether it be more money, reputation, or accumulation in general. would i be no better in their shoes? is this the intended byproduct of the systems built “for” us? leaves a bad taste in my mouth

items.content_html:
中銀膠囊大樓 Nakagin Capsule Tower

1970-1972 日本, 東京 Tokyo, Japan

Located in the heart of Tokyo, Kurokawa Kisho’s Nakagin Capsule Tower housed 140 self-contained units. The small apartments were designed for short-term stays by people who worked in the urban centre while living in the suburbs, reflecting new trends in how people moved throughout the city. The capsules were marketed as additional office space, secondary residences, or simple sites to recharge near the workplace. The tower was one of the few buildings realised as part of the 1960s Japanese architectural movement known as Metabolism. The name of the movement was a biological metaphor for how architecture could be designed with the ability to evolve, accommodating growth and changing societal needs. Attached to a concrete core service tower, the Nakagin capsules could, in theory, be replaced, which would extend the overall lifespan of the building. However, the building fell into disrepair in the early 2000s.

Despite numerous attempts to save it, it was demolished in 2022. Some capsules were carefully restored and collected by museums around the world, such as Unit A806 at M+.

June 10th, 2025 / M+ / West Kowloon, Hong Kong

items.content_html:
Region No. 43701-No. 43900 (1998) LED mounted on aluminium, circuitry

Miyajima Tatsuo born 1957, Japan works Ibaraki

Two hundred LED counters flash numbers between 1 and 99 in red and green in endless loops. After reaching 99, the counter returns to 1. Numbers with the digit 0, a symbol of finality and emptiness for the artist, are omitted. The work may evoke affectless computer code but was in fact inspired by Miyajima’s experiences in the hospitals he frequented as a chronically ill child. The continual flashing and counting of numbers illustrate the Buddhist concept of samsara, the ceaseless cycle of reincarnation.

June 10, 2025 / M+ / West Kowloon, Hong Kong

This work comprises photographs of morning staff assemblies at over forty shops in Chinese cities, including Shanghai and Shenzhen. Zhou Tao edits and arranges the images according to the rhythm of the chants, showing how the collectivity of a socialist past has acquired a new function in the market economy as a highly effective governing tactic for modern corporations.

likes

  • tidbit on stationary: i have too, too, too much T.T
  • COOL TECH GADGETS THAT ARE GENUINELY USEFUL EVEN IF ITS NICHE-LY USEFUL AND NOT CHEAP LANDFILL STUFF (ik it’s kinda pricey for good, useful gadgets, which will probably populate my specific items list below, so it’s really not expected… genuinely this wishlist is not even being shared to people as i honestly don’t know who would get me thoughtful gifts, or gifts in general, outside like 2 people—for better or worse, probably the latter LOL, so anything would be such such a pleasant surprise!)
  • oooo books!!! the books i usually carry/like are sci-fi, cooking, and personal interests: interior design, architecture, tiny homes, japanese minimalism, etc. but im always open to more!
  • urban transit / planning stuff is always cool!!
  • your time + thoughtfulness is honestly the greatest gift. it’s not easy and convenient, and i genuinely understand, which is why i truly truly appreciate it <3

caution

  • cheap, low-effort gifts: i’ve received like really bad half-minded gifts that looked like they’re from knockoff amazon, and yes i get it. something is better than nothing, but honestly i would 100% appreciate thoughtful card or some of your time over coffee/tea over that although i know those options takes intentionality and effort still, which is what a cheap, low-effort gift is supposed to escape from. like i dont mean to be ungrateful, and i really appreciate the minute thought and act of getting a gift of course, but i just would really want to avoid contributing to global waste by having to toss junk out. like as much as i want to say i appreciate the sentiment, i just really unappreciate that kind of something over nothing!
  • no. more. plushies. i really cannot accommodate additional ones, so they will be donated to kiddos + anyone/anywhere else that would be a good home for them!

specific wishes: very non-encompassing

  • vinyls!!! (japanese city pop, soft alt rnb like joji/keshi, arctic monkeys, ATLA soundtracks, not sure what else rn)
  • meta ray-ban glasses gen 3 (~$300) it’s not out yet though, gen 1 and 2 are out, but 3 should come late 2025 or early 2026!! or some kind of smart glasses in general. i don’t fancy meta tbh, esp. in our generation of social media addiction + the ease and enablement of disinformation, misinformation, propaganda, and more by just throwing money around
  • contributions to my FIRE journey 🙏🙏🙏
  • quality power bank w/ built-in usb-c (10k+ mAh) for ex: this anker one :D (added 11/16/25)

thank you’s:

  • october 2025 (to gabi): for all the small gifties everywhere, like making lunch onigiris, paying for all sorts of random things here and there, helping us get rid of our excess “stuff”, the blue shirt and brown sweater from malaysia (very very appreciated c: i really like quality, well-fitting clothing as gifts), and anything else i missed
  • september 2025 (to myself): airpod pros 3, you were so needed, been waiting for you to come out ever since someone stole my 2’s and brought them to new york city
  • fall 2025 (to muslima): thank you for the photobook of our trip in japan. it was such a thoughtful gift, and i also really liked the cat stickers that were included as well :D

items.content_html:
I feel like there’s a lot to unpack, yet I’m still in the same constantly-on mode as I was this whole semester. It’s hard for me to really think, like there’s some kind of invisible weight on the top of my head. I think I’ll wait until later this summer to slowly let out some thoughts.

Just wanted to at least put an update out, especially since I’m not doing really anything at this particular minute.

This past week, though, has been hectic. Had to:

  • Take over repairs and maintenance for the condo I grew up in as parents have long been pretty mid + unbothered landlords and neglecting some much needed work: talked quotes, soothed frustrated residents, negotiated w/ contractors, coordinated HOA for water shut-offs, trying to figure out whether I’m getting a fair price or not, ensuring contract was somewhat bullet-resistant, taking initiative w/ gestures of goodwill, and just constant CALLS, CALLS, CALLS. However, the work should finish up tomorrow or the day after, which will hopefully offer some much-needed reprieve. Not sure if I’ll write up something about this, but tl;dr is old type-m cheap copper pipes, pinhole leaks -> water damage, doing full repipe w/ PEX-A + adaptors, issues w/ sharing lines, + drywall restoration.
  • Help w/ my mom’s car repairs. Was making a pretty bad noise + driving poorly. I advised her to go to a trusted local/independent mechanic rather than a dealership, and I even sent a few over to her that I vetted. She ended up at the dealership, but luckily, it was a pretty reasonably-priced inspection, and I was able to convince her to take the repairs at a trusted mechanic, which saved over $1000 overall. There could’ve been a few upsells like air filters, but honestly well-priced ones, so why not. They might’ve genuinely needed a change + it’s not like my parents would change those themselves. Win-win in my books. They get a bit more business + we get good prices on the larger repairs like changing the brake rotors and pads that she wore down.
  • Follow up on my two student’s college things, which I need to do later today as well, as they’re not staying on top of registration and other tasks despite promises to do so. I love working with them, but goodness it’s frustrating because I can’t be there for them all the time.
  • Catching up with United work: set up laptop for better access to Foundry + heads down/deep work. Lots and lots to do and figure out, sighs.
  • Parents came over for general commencement + broke the PS5 and showerhead within the 20 hours they stayed at the house, so had to get those repaired. Shopped around for PS5 hdmi repair quotes (ranged from $150-180) and found this goated shop that gave me a student discount to total $88 after taxes. Shoutout Quickfix Wireless on Telegraph. Evan (LL and roommate) handled the showerhead, ty.
  • Packing + moving + parents + graduation + social + dinners/chats w/ ppl’s parents + all of that. Not really stressful like the rest, but rather the fun and freeing side of the week.
  • IPIRA + RDI, need to get a move on those.
  • Final grades are rolling out. One professor mixed me up with another “Chen” and gave me a B instead of an A-. Actually had me so pmo for the last 24 hours, but he resolved it, thank goodness. Thought I needed to file a grade appeal or something for the first time in my college career because that was the most unwarranted B I ever gotten. In comparison, I’m happy to settle with an A-. After all, this professor is notorious with random grading that favors student athletes, finance bros/gals, and his inner circle of students. I, for one, am not part of that, but I did my fair share of the participation and work, so an A- is honestly quite reasonable. As for CS61C, I think I ended with a B+, which was better than my original hope for a B-, yet falls just short of an A-. Given I learned almost 75% of the course content in the two weeks leading up to the final. It’s a fair B+. Had I put in some effort into the class besides the bare minimum throughout the semester, I think I would have gotten an A-, although one could argue I wouldn’t have studied as hard as I did had I not been and justifiably felt so unprepared for the final. Seeing if I can clutch up an A-, but I think I’m, again, just short of the cut-off. Can’t have it all haha. Should be happy with what I have and how I did on the exam tbh. Went from -0.55 z-score to a positive one, which then clobbered the bad midterm performance.
  • Still tutoring, too :P

Anyways, a little psychological analysis if you don’t mind. Apparently, I’m (as well as many others for sure) in this state of cognitive fatigue and decision overload, a state where my prefrontal cortex (responsible for planning, focusing, and regulating emotions) is worn down from a long period of sustained mental effort. Like muscle fatigue, but for executive function. So, brain is genuinely exhausted. Additionally, chronic stress hormones are still being produced as our bodies have been running on cortisol and adrenaline for months, so that fight or flight is still basically on. Makes it hard to feel peace, rest, or process emotions. There’s also this psychological transition lag that psychologists call “liminal space” (an in-between zone after one identity ends (student) and before the next fully forms (adult/corporate cog/etc?). And apparently the brain dislikes this uncertainty and loss of structure, so it creates a weird emotional “buzz” where things can feel frozen or numb. Last concept would be the rest paradox, where rest after being in the hustle mode long enough can feel quite uncomfortable and even stressful as my brain associates idleness with being “unproductive” so it keeps scanning for tasks, making it hard to decompress. However, it’s right though as I do have a lot of tasks still, even after graduating, which I find ridiculous T.T let me travel and relax already.

All of it should pass with time as the nervous system rebalances and I actually finish some of the tasks on my plate :)

“Rest is not idleness, and to lie sometimes on the grass under trees on a summer’s day, listening to the murmur of the water, or watching the clouds float across the sky, is by no means a waste of time.” ― John Lubbock, The Use Of Life

just studying for cs61c, going to be a really tough final; perhaps the toughest in my undergrad career simply due to the lack of preparation, discipline, and prioritization

reaping what i sow… it’s genuinely such an interesting class, but just have a sizable amount on my plate the entire semester, sighs. however, now on lecture 38, guest speaker Dave Patterson from Google and UC Berkeley

lessons from the first 50 years of my career

People

  1. Family first! Don’t sacrifice your family’s happiness on the altar of success.
  2. Choose happiness.
  3. It’s the people, not the projects, that you value in the long run.
  4. The cost of praise is small. The value to others is inestimable.
  5. Seek out honest feedback; it might be right.
  6. “For better or for worse, benchmarks shape a field.”
  7. “I learned that courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it.”
  8. Beware of those who believe that they are the smartest person in the room.

Career

  1. “Most of us spend too much time on what is urgent and not enough time on what is important.”
  2. “Nothing great in the world has ever been accomplished without passion.”
  3. “There are no losers on a winning team, and no winners on a losing team.”
  4. Lead by example.
  5. “Audentes Fortuna iuvat.” (Fortune favors the bold).
  6. Culture matters.
  7. It’s not how many projects you start; it’s how many you finish.
  8. Look for the positive opportunities.

Saw this random tweet on Instagram, who knows if it’s true and it doesn’t really matter to me either. Basically, the question was: can somebody explain the logic of waiting until you have the red to cross the street?

A person said: When my mother first moved to Japan, she tried to jaywalk while pushing a stroller on an empty residential street. She was immediately stopped by an old, well-dressed Japanese man who solemnly told her in perfect English “the downfall of society begins with the individual”

There’s a lot of truth to that statement, yet I find some of the pushback quite relatable, like the frustration of a world increasingly dominated by cars. Collectivism and individualism is also a key conflict. As much as I like individualism to whatever extent my understanding is, it saddens me to see the lack of unity and collectivism in my country. But, back to the topic at hand, jaywalking is fine in many instances. There’s a lot of empty streets in Japan that locals still wait for the green light for. There’s also a lot of empty streets in which they don’t wait for the light. I think there’s a few factors that come into play with that decision for locals. As for me, I just follow what the locals do tbh. If they wait, I’ll wait. If they don’t I don’t. However, I agree that streets should be for the people. The way we move around the city should center around pedestrians first.

There’s a lot more depth to this issue that I’m not covering, of course. Why do lights exist? Why is jaywalking considered bad? etc. This isn’t a fully flushed-out thought, just a random one. (rediscovered for myself a really iconic illustration below)

items.content_html: finished All Quiet on the Western Front today for my NLP class. honestly really appreciated the excuse to read. it was nice not having to worry about not advancing my academic backlog of work and be able to enjoy a nice book. I have wondered oftentimes whether reading a book is similar to watching a tv show, especially if both are fiction. but having not truly read in a while, I can see the benefits of being exposed to more varied, thoughtful, intentional, and creative writing. what a shame that we’re transitioning into a world that no longer substantially rewards those who practice and master the art of writing. in high school, I longed to write as eloquently as the authors I was subjected to read. now, despite my understanding that effort spent is not wasted, it still feels like a waste to devote oneself to a skill so easily mimicked mindlessly. of course, it’s not 100% the same, but even 80% is a skill level largely attainable traditionally through trying practice and time. I can’t even begin to sympathize for artists and designers out there. of course, there are many that can take advantage of newer technologies to grow and succeed. perhaps this is simply another blip in the march of technological growth and its impact. but one can’t seem to pause and consider what might be lost in the process for our generations today.

items.content_html:
ok why does everything cost money?

so went to get my smog checked, $30 regardless if pass or fail failed, obviously by the title, and it’s because error code P0012 - “A” Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Retarded Bank 1. just great because I diagnosed this issue months and months ago and found that it’s not only a common problem on the Miata NB, but also very hard to find the root cause…

ok so after an hour dooming and researching outside because I can’t sell my car without passing smog. I found the California CAP (consumer assistance program) which can help cover costs of repair up to X amount if I qualify. well I’m on CalFresh so I do, but it’s a joint ownership so I’m worried my mom will disqualify mimi for it. sighs.

anyways I went to a cafe to collect my thoughts bc the smog check place said it’d be $150 for diagnosis.

I called Fred’s Warehouse and didn’t really know what to say tbh. kinda out of my field of expertise. are they able to diagnose over the phone? is there even a point telling him my error code? like what?? anyways he was a bit stern but nice and straightforward, said that I should check my oil as a first measure since it can affect the camshaft position. that I knew but I guess I got overwhelmed by the tens and tens of other issues that could cause this error code on mimi. also he said $175 for diagnosis, pain.

so I was like okay, let’s oil change mimi myself bc I should learn anyways and I like doing DIY. but tell me why miata owners say the oil/filter the most inconveniently located place for NB?! also I don’t want to hurt myself, hurt the car, and have a mess to deal with like waste oil. so yeah, it was not worth my time right now as I’m a college student without much time nor tools. sooooo, looked at places to get my oil changed and I was like might as well get my leaking tire fixed.

so tires. I called DC Tires bc a AAA mechanic brought gabi and mimi there once to get a new tire and apparently a really good experience + good price. they were indeed nice and said they got nothing that old in stock, that being 24 years old model. fair. they recommended me to buy a tire online and they can switch it for me. as for oil change, they didn’t do it but referred me to an oil change shop, which would top off my other fluids, too. not sure what other fluids there are tbh. i know there are other fluids, but how good is that deal persay.

anyways, my smog test place also did oil changes and they were nice. $60 was their quote, but they told me to first check if I need a top-off or an oil change, and that I shouldn’t do an oil change if unnecessary. hence why I like that place in general, solid advice. so, I guess that’s the next step. something about a dipstick and oil level. sighs.

the nice reprieve is that all these places (DC, Fred’s, and 15min) seemed pretty helpful and considerate and gave me tips to move towards resolving the issues I brought up w/o necessarily trying to upsell me their services. for that, I am quite appreciative, esp. given the poor reputation the mechanic/car industry as a whole has in their treatment and exploitation of the uninformed and poor.

registration apparently expiring in two days, what to do. got an exam that day, too, which I’m behind on, so that takes priority. being broke is tough. but just fyi, at least in cali, I already paid the registration fee so I won’t get charged late fees, but when my tag expires in the two days, I can technically get pulled over and get fix-it tickets, which should be resolved once I, yk, fix the problem in question. impt thing is: avoid public parking. apparently u can just get parking tickets for incomplete registration, which is the case here. sighs.

“it is expensive to be poor” - james baldwin

so I was like okay, let's oil change mimi myself bc I should learn anyways and I like doing DIY. but tell me why miata owners say the oil/filter the most inconveniently located place for NB?! also I don't want to hurt myself, hurt the car, and have a mess to deal with like waste oil. so yeah, it was not worth my time right now as I'm a college student without much time nor tools. sooooo, looked at places to get my oil changed and I was like might as well get my leaking tire fixed. 

so tires. I called DC Tires bc a AAA mechanic brought gabi and mimi there once to get a new tire and apparently a really good experience + good price. they were indeed nice and said they got nothing that old in stock, that being 24 years old model. fair. they recommended me to buy a tire online and they can switch it for me. as for oil change, they didn't do it but referred me to an oil change shop, which would top off my other fluids, too. not sure what other fluids there are tbh. i know there are other fluids, but how good is that deal persay.

anyways, my smog test place also did oil changes and they were nice. $60 was their quote, but they told me to first check if I need a top-off or an oil change, and that I shouldn't do an oil change if unnecessary.  hence why I like that place in general, solid advice. so, I guess that's the next step. something about a dipstick and oil level. sighs.

the nice reprieve is that all these places (DC, Fred's, and 15min) seemed pretty helpful and considerate and gave me tips to move towards resolving the issues I brought up w/o necessarily trying to upsell me their services. for that, I am quite appreciative, esp. given the poor reputation the mechanic/car industry as a whole has in their treatment and exploitation of the uninformed and poor.

registration apparently expiring in two days, what to do. got an exam that day, too, which I'm behind on, so that takes priority. being broke is tough. but just fyi, at least in cali, I already paid the registration fee so I won't get charged late fees, but when my tag expires in the two days, I can technically get pulled over and get fix-it tickets, which should be resolved once I, yk, fix the problem in question. impt thing is: avoid public parking. apparently u can just get parking tickets for incomplete registration, which is the case here. sighs.

**"it is expensive to be poor" - james baldwin**
